# Abstract {-}

Romania's 2024–2025 electoral cycle produced historic parliamentary fragmentation
and the unexpected rise of nationalist-populist candidates, culminating in a
second-round presidential contest between George Simion and Elena Lasconi-Dan.
Using official county-level (*județ*) data for all 42 NUTS-3 units and a
multi-method analytical framework, this paper documents seven empirical findings.

(1) Romanian counties organise into five structurally coherent voter-profile
clusters stable under alternative $k \in \{4,6\}$ specifications (ARI $\geq 0.72$);
deindustrialisation is the dominant cross-party structural predictor in a Dirichlet
regression of vote share composition (five terms survive Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
correction at $q = 0.10$); and ethnic composition is the sharpest single-party
predictor. The annulment of Georgescu's 2024 result left no detectable county-level
mobilisation fingerprint on Simion R1 turnout ($r_{\text{partial}} = -0.123$,
$p = 0.437$).
(2) The nationalist-populist electoral bloc defined by Georgescu's 2024 first-round
support shows a partial county-level correlation of $r = 0.770$ with Simion's 2025
first-round support after controlling for eight structural confounders
(Robustness Value = 0.547), confirming bloc persistence independent of geography.
(3) AUR's 2020–2024 Senate swing is substantially explained by demographic pressure
($R^2 = 0.585$); under a centred log-ratio compositional specification the sign
and significance pattern is directionally consistent, validating the finding under
Aitchison geometry. A spatial lag model (GM two-stage, $\hat{\rho} = 0.640$) raises
pseudo-$R^2$ to 0.707 and confirms that AUR mobilisation has a neighbourhood
contagion component beyond shared structural conditions.
(4) Romania's permanent electoral rolls inflate by a mean of 16.4\% relative to
the estimated adult resident population, almost entirely predicted by emigration
rates ($R^2 = 0.680$); ghost electorate inflation deflates reported turnout by
a mean of 9.1 percentage points but does not independently predict cross-county
turnout variation once structural controls are included ($p = 0.262$).
(5) Dan's 2025 runoff consolidation of the anti-Simion pool was most efficient
in ethnically mixed Transylvania (ratio = 0.953) and weakest in the most deprived
flatland cluster (0.823), consistent with a defensive rather than programmatic coalition.
(6) A Bayesian hierarchical reformulation of the AUR swing model (4 chains
$\times$ 4000 draws, nutpie backend; max R-hat $= 1.001$, min ESS $= 4{,}461$)
confirms long-term unemployment as the sole positive structural predictor of AUR
growth (posterior mean $= +0.015$, 90\% CI $[+0.005, +0.025]$) while revealing
that higher composite grievance is associated with *lower* AUR swing
(posterior mean $= -0.029$, 90\% CI $[-0.045, -0.013]$) — a paradox resolved
by distinguishing aspirationally disappointed deindustrialised counties from
the worst-off counties where electoral fatalism suppresses nationalist mobilisation.
Under the 2025 structural geography and calibrated bloc transfer rates, a
conditional projection places the mean Simion second-round share at 47.1\%
(90\% PI: 44.9\%–49.2\%), with 9 of 42 counties in genuine uncertainty.

**Keywords:** Romanian elections, Dirichlet regression, electoral geography,
deindustrialisation, spatial autocorrelation, ghost electorate, compositional data,
Bayesian hierarchical model, conditional projection.

# Introduction

Romania's December 2024 parliamentary elections and the subsequent 2025 presidential
re-run produced an electoral landscape with no precedent in the post-communist period.
The radical-right Alliance for Romania's Unity (AUR) consolidated its position as
the second largest parliamentary force; the nationalist SOS România entered parliament
for the first time; and Călin Georgescu's first-round presidential result —
subsequently annulled by the Constitutional Court — demonstrated the mobilisation
potential of diffuse online-networked populism outside traditional party structures.

Two questions motivate this study. *What structural conditions differentiate counties
that produced high nationalist-populist vote shares from those that did not?* And
*to what extent does county-level support for Georgescu in November 2024 predict
support for George Simion in May 2025, net of shared structural characteristics?*

We approach both questions with compositional and partial-correlation methods that
respect the constrained nature of vote shares and guard against confounding through
systematic covariate adjustment.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section \@ref(sec:data) describes the data sources
and variable construction. Section \@ref(sec:clustering) presents the voter profile
typology. Section \@ref(sec:dirichlet) reports the Dirichlet regression of party
vote shares. Section \@ref(sec:transfer) quantifies the Georgescu–Simion transfer.
Section \@ref(sec:temporal) analyses the 2020–2024 parliamentary swing and
the 2024–2025 presidential arc. Section \@ref(sec:ghost) examines the ghost
electorate. Section \@ref(sec:spatial) provides spatial robustness checks.
Section \@ref(sec:confessional) decomposes the aggregate Magyar share predictor
into seven denomination z-scores and tests confessional mobilisation hypotheses.
Section \@ref(sec:robustness) assesses sensitivity to the cluster granularity choice.
Section \@ref(sec:projections) develops conditional projections under three
explicit structural assumptions. Section \@ref(sec:discussion) discusses the
findings in the context of comparative populism research.
Section \@ref(sec:conclusion) concludes with limitations and directions for
future work.

# Data and Measurement {#sec:data}

## Electoral outcomes

Parliamentary vote shares for the December 2024 elections were obtained from the
Permanent Electoral Authority (AEP). We model eight compositional outcomes:
AUR, PSD, PNL, USR, UDMR, SOS, POT, and a residual *Other* category.
All shares were reweighted to sum to exactly one after excluding invalid ballots.
Presidential first-round results for Călin Georgescu (November 2024) and
George Simion (May 2025) were sourced from the same authority.

## Structural predictors

County-level structural characteristics were assembled from three sources:

- **Eurostat NUTS-3 database** (2022 reference year): GDP per capita, unemployment
  rate, household income (PPS), long-term unemployment rate, industry GVA share,
  early school leaving, tertiary education, net and temporary emigration rates,
  infrastructure density, and religious/ethnic composition from the 2021 census.
- **Romanian National Statistics Institute (INS)**: population density,
  age structure, employment by sector, healthcare and school unit density,
  urbanisation, and household size.
- **Derived indices**: The *grievance index* ($\overline{z}$ of unemployment,
  poverty risk, early school leaving, and long-term unemployment, reversed for
  income), the *modernity index* ($\overline{z}$ of tertiary education, internet
  use, and GDP per capita), and the *deindustrialisation index*
  (industry GVA share 2010 − industry GVA share 2022, clipped at zero).

The deindustrialisation index captures counties where manufacturing activity has
contracted since 2010, consistent with the spatial polarisation literature on
post-communist industrial legacy [@Nölke2009; @Bohle2012].

## Variable transformation

All continuous structural predictors were standardised ($z$-scores) to permit
direct comparison of coefficient magnitudes. Compositional vote shares were
closed to the unit simplex and passed to `DR_data()` for Dirichlet regression,
which applies a small perturbation to exact zeros and ones [@Maier2014].

# Voter Profile Typology {#sec:clustering}

## Method

We apply Ward hierarchical clustering [@Ward1963] in the eight-dimensional PCA
space of 34 standardised structural features. PCA retains components explaining
at least 80% of total variance (eight components in this dataset). Clustering in
PCA space reduces the influence of highly correlated raw features without
subjective variable exclusion.

The number of clusters was selected by bootstrap stability analysis
[@Hennig2007]: we define stability as the mean adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between
pairs of bootstrap cluster solutions. A threshold of ARI $\geq 0.85$ is used to
classify a partition as *strongly stable*. The gap statistic [@Tibshirani2001]
consistently returned $k = 1$ for this dataset, which we attribute to the
smooth continuum of development gradients across Romanian counties; we therefore
rely on bootstrap ARI as the primary selection criterion.

$k = 5$ emerges as the smallest strongly stable partition
(bootstrap ARI = 0.854) and is preferred on theoretical grounds over $k = 3$,
which conflates structurally distinct regions.

## Results

```{r fig-dendrogram, fig.cap="Ward hierarchical clustering dendrogram — 34 structural features, $k=5$ cut. County labels coloured by cluster assignment."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "06c_dendrogram_final.png"))
```

```{r fig-biplot, fig.cap="PCA biplot with $k=5$ cluster overlay. Arrows indicate the six features with highest PC1 loadings. PC1 (horizontal) separates peripheral-agricultural from urban-industrial counties; PC2 (vertical) separates the ethnic-mosaic northwest."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "06c_pca_biplot_final.png"))
```

The five clusters are described below and summarised in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-heatmap).

**C1 — Moldova Profundă** (*n* = 6): Bacău, Botoșani, Iași, Neamț, Suceava, Vaslui.
The highest agricultural employment (+1.38 SD), lowest GDP (−0.81 SD), and
highest emigration rates. The defining structural signature is precarity through
agricultural marginalisation rather than industrial collapse.

**C2 — Câmpia Uitată** (*n* = 17): The largest cluster, covering most of
Wallachia and Dobrogea. Moderate GDP, lower deindustrialisation than expected
(−0.47 SD) because energy and petrochemical rents have maintained a residual
industry GVA share. The structural analogue to the Western European "left-behind"
periphery [@Rodríguez-Pose2018], but attenuated by sectoral rents.

**C3 — Insula Capitalei** (*n* = 2): București and Ilfov. An extreme outlier
on GDP (+4.24 SD), household income (+3.98 SD), and urbanisation (+1.87 SD).
Represents the capital-region concentration typical of Eastern European
developmental states [@Iammarino2019].

**C4 — Centrele Dinamice** (*n* = 9): Alba, Arad, Brașov, Caraș-Severin,
Cluj, Constanța, Hunedoara, Sibiu, Timiș. High industry GVA share (+1.42 SD)
reflecting FDI-led automotive and electronics manufacturing. The one cluster
where industrial employment is growing rather than contracting.

**C5 — Arcul Identitar** (*n* = 8): Bihor, Bistrița-Năsăud, Covasna, Harghita,
Maramureș, Mureș, Satu Mare, Sălaj. Distinguished by ethnic diversity
(Magyar-speaking minority, Reformed and Greco-Catholic denominations) and moderate
deindustrialisation (+0.60 SD). The UDMR ethnic bloc vote is structurally encoded
in this cluster.

```{r fig-heatmap, fig.cap="Z-scored cluster means on 24 key structural features. Red = above-average, blue = below-average."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "06c_heatmap_final.png"))
```

## Cluster validation

One-way ANOVA on held-out electoral variables (not used in clustering) confirms
significant between-cluster variation for all major parties
(AUR: $F = 9.11$, $p < 0.001$; PSD: $F = 12.34$, $p < 0.001$;
USR: $F = 13.96$, $p < 0.001$; UDMR: $F = 12.15$, $p < 0.001$).
PNL is the sole exception ($F = 0.50$, $p = 0.74$), consistent with its
cross-regional catch-all positioning.

```{r fig-vote-profiles, fig.cap="Cluster-mean electoral profiles for held-out 2024 parliamentary and presidential variables."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "06c_vote_profiles_final.png"))
```

# Compositional Analysis of Vote Shares {#sec:dirichlet}

## Dirichlet regression

Vote shares constitute compositional data: they are strictly positive, sum to one,
and carry information only as ratios relative to each other
[@Aitchison1986; @Pawlowsky-Glahn2015]. Separate OLS regressions on each party
violate the simplex constraint and ignore cross-party covariance. We instead
model the joint composition $\mathbf{Y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_8)$ as a Dirichlet
response:

$$\mathbf{Y} \sim \text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}), \quad
\alpha_k = \mu_k \cdot \phi, \quad
\log\!\left(\frac{\mu_k}{\mu_K}\right) = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}_k$$

where $\phi$ is a common precision parameter shared across categories
("common" parameterisation; @Maier2014), $K = 8$ (*Other*) is the reference
category, and $\mathbf{x}$ contains standardised structural predictors.
Coefficients are on the additive log-ratio (ALR) scale: a positive $\hat{\beta}_k$
indicates that a one-SD increase in the predictor is associated with a higher
share for party $k$ *relative to* the Other category.

We fit two nested models:

- **M1**: $\mathbf{Y} \sim$ grievance + modernity + \% Magyar + deindustrialisation
  ($p = 4$, 40 parameters)
- **M2**: M1 + demographic pressure + \% Roma + long-term unemployment
  ($p = 7$, 64 parameters)

Given $N = 42$, M1 represents the upper boundary of estimable model complexity
for full standard-error recovery. M2 is included as a model-comparison benchmark
via likelihood-ratio test; standard errors are unavailable due to Hessian
non-convergence at this sample size.

```{r dirichlet-fit-table}
# Build model comparison table from stored results
fit_tab <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Log-lik.`, ~AIC,    ~`N params`, ~`LR stat`, ~`LR $p$`, ~`Maddala $R^2$`,
  "Null", "304.7",    "—",      "8",         "—",         "—",       "—",
  "M1",   "639.2",   "−1198",   "40",        "334.6",    "<0.001",  "1.000",
  "M2",   "718.4",   "−1309",   "64",        "492.9",    "<0.001",  "1.000"
)

knitr::kable(
  fit_tab,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Dirichlet regression model fit statistics. LR stat = $2(\\ell_\\text{full} - \\ell_\\text{null})$. Maddala $R^2 = 1 - \\exp(-\\text{LR}/N)$.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

## Coefficient results

```{r dirichlet-coef-table}
coef_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "08a_dirichlet_coefs.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)

sig_m1 <- coef_df |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "M1", term != "(Intercept)", !is.na(p), p < 0.10) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Party     = sub("t_", "", category),
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(term,
      z_grievance    = "Grievance Index",
      z_modernity    = "Modernity Index",
      z_magyari      = "\\% Magyar",
      z_deindustrial = "Deindustrialisation"
    ),
    `$\\hat{\\beta}$` = sprintf("%.3f",  estimate),
    SE                 = sprintf("%.3f",  se),
    `$z$`             = sprintf("%.2f",  z),
    `$p$`             = dplyr::case_when(
      p < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE      ~ sprintf("%.3f", p)
    ),
    Sig = as.character(sig)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(p) |>
  dplyr::select(Party, Predictor, `$\\hat{\\beta}$`, SE, `$z$`, `$p$`, Sig)

knitr::kable(
  sig_m1,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "M1 Dirichlet regression: significant predictors ($p < 0.10$), ordered by $p$-value. Coefficients on ALR scale (reference = Other). All predictors standardised.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dirichlet-coefs) visualises the full M1 coefficient matrix.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-dirichlet-fit) assesses model calibration.

```{r fig-dirichlet-coefs, fig.cap="M1 Dirichlet regression coefficients with 95\\% confidence intervals. Coefficients on ALR scale relative to the Other category. Faded points: $p > 0.05$."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "08a_dirichlet_coefs.png"))
```

```{r fig-dirichlet-fit, fig.cap="M2 fitted vs observed vote shares by party, coloured by voter-profile cluster. Diagonal = perfect calibration."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "08a_dirichlet_fitted_obs.png"))
```

```

## Interpretation

Three patterns stand out.

*Deindustrialisation is the dominant cross-party structural signal.* The
deindustrialisation index carries a positive and significant coefficient for
every party except UDMR (Table \@ref(tab:dirichlet-coef-table)), indicating that
counties that lost industrial share since 2010 have compositionally shifted away
from the residual Other category toward all named parties. This is not a
party-specific effect but a general activation of partisan choice in formerly
industrial territories — consistent with the "places that don't matter" thesis
[@Rodríguez-Pose2018] applied to the post-communist context.

*Ethnic composition is the sharpest single-party predictor.* The Magyar share
coefficient for UDMR ($\hat{\beta} = 1.026$, SE = 0.136, $p < 10^{-13}$) dwarfs
all other point estimates in absolute magnitude, confirming the ethnic bloc
character of UDMR's electorate. The coefficient is four to five times larger
than the next-largest significant estimate, consistent with the near-deterministic
nature of minority bloc voting at the ecological level.

*Modernity differentiates the remaining bloc.* Higher modernity is associated
with lower SOS share ($\hat{\beta} = -0.326$, $p = 0.027$) and higher UDMR
share ($\hat{\beta} = 0.675$, $p = 0.021$, reflecting UDMR's urban concentration
in Transylvanian cities). The grievance index, by contrast, has no significant
net effect on any party's share once structural predictors are controlled,
suggesting that the spatial distribution of grievance does not map cleanly onto
a single electoral outlet.

*PNL's structural invariance* — confirmed by non-significant ANOVA ($F = 0.50$,
$p = 0.74$) and absence from the significant-predictor table — is consistent with
its catch-all, brokerage positioning across regional contexts.

## Multiple testing and FDR correction

With 32 non-intercept coefficient tests across 8 outcome categories in M1, familywise
error control is important. Applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
[@Benjamini1995] at a false discovery rate threshold of $q = 0.10$, five terms
survive correction: Magyar share on UDMR ($q < 0.001$), deindustrialisation on
POT ($q = 0.015$), PSD ($q = 0.067$), USR ($q = 0.096$), and Other ($q = 0.096$).
The Magyar–UDMR relationship is thus extremely robust to multiplicity adjustment,
while the deindustrialisation signal for the populist and residual parties survives
at acceptable FDR. The modernity and grievance coefficients, individually
suggestive at $p < 0.10$, do not survive FDR correction.

## Leave-one-out cross-validation

To assess predictive generalisability at $N = 42$, we compute leave-one-out
Aitchison distance between held-out observed composition and M1 predicted composition,
comparing to a null model that always predicts the grand-mean composition
[@Aitchison1986]. A LOO skill score of 0 indicates no improvement over the null;
1 indicates perfect prediction. M1 achieves a skill score of **0.179**
(mean Aitchison distance: M1 = 3.675, null = 4.474), indicating modest but positive
predictive skill beyond the mean-composition baseline. The low absolute skill
reflects the difficulty of extrapolating compositional predictions at this sample
size — M1 should be interpreted as a structural description rather than a
forecasting model.

## ALR marginal effects in share space

Because Dirichlet coefficients are on the ALR scale, we translate them to
percentage-point effects on predicted vote shares by perturbing each predictor
by $+1$ SD at the grand mean of all predictors and computing the implied
change in predicted composition. Table \@ref(tab:marginal-effects-table) reports
these marginal effects.

```{r marginal-effects-table}
me_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "08c_dirichlet_marginal_effects.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)

me_display <- me_df |>
  dplyr::rename(Predictor = predictor) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Predictor = gsub("%", "\\\\%", Predictor)) |>
  dplyr::rename_with(~ gsub("^t_", "", .x), dplyr::starts_with("t_"))

knitr::kable(
  me_display,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits   = 2,
  caption  = "ALR marginal effects: predicted vote share change (pp) per $+1$ SD in each predictor, evaluated at grand-mean structural values. Computed from M1 coefficients.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```

The marginal effects confirm the substantive picture from the ALR coefficients:
a one-SD increase in the Magyar share is associated with a $+6.3$ pp gain for UDMR
and roughly offsetting losses of $-3.6$ pp for PSD, $-1.2$ pp for AUR, and $-1.1$ pp
for POT. Deindustrialisation shifts $+1.3$ pp toward POT and $+0.9$ pp toward PSD
while modestly compressing AUR ($-0.7$ pp), consistent with POT acting as a more
localised industrial-protest outlet than AUR in the composition.

## Confessional decomposition {#sec:confessional}

The aggregate Magyar share variable in M1 absorbs what is, in the census data, a
confessionally bimodal community: ethnic Hungarians in Romania are predominantly
Reformed Calvinist (≈45\% of Hungarian speakers) and Roman Catholic (≈40\%),
with a Unitarian minority (≈5\%) concentrated in Harghita.
We decompose this signal by replacing \texttt{pct\_maghiari} with seven
denomination z-scores — Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Reformed, Pentecostal,
Greek Catholic, Unitarian, and a secular bloc (atheist + agnostic + no religion
+ undeclared) — sourced from INS RPL2021 Table 2.5.2, and refit the ALR model.

```{r confessional-lr-table}
lr_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "15a_confessional_lr_test.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  lr_df |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      `Model A` = gsub("_", "\\\\_", model_a),
      `Model B` = gsub("_", "\\\\_", model_b),
      `$\\chi^2$` = round(chi2, 2),
      df = df,
      `$p$` = ifelse(p < 0.001, "$<$0.001", sprintf("%.4f", p))
    ),
  booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
  caption = "Likelihood-ratio test: confessional model (7 denominations) vs.~original M1 (aggregate Magyar share). df~=~7 extra parameters $\\times$ 7 ALR equations."
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 9)
```

```{r fig-confessional-heatmap, fig.cap="Confessional decomposition: ALR coefficient heatmap (7 denominations $\\times$ 7 parties, Other = reference). Cells marked * survive BH-FDR at $q < 0.10$. Colour scale: red = positive association, blue = negative."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "15a_confessional_heatmap.png"))
```

The LR test favours $M_{\text{conf}}$ strongly ($\chi^2(49) = 138.6$, $p < 0.001$),
indicating that the confessional structure contains information beyond the single
aggregate ethnic variable. However, the three pre-registered denominational
hypotheses are all null after BH-FDR correction.

**H1 (UDMR ~ Reformed and Roman Catholic)** — neither Reformed
($\hat{\beta} = -0.14$, $p = 0.894$) nor Roman Catholic
($\hat{\beta} = -0.46$, $p = 0.752$) is individually significant for UDMR,
despite the model achieving $R^2 = 0.935$. The high $R^2$ alongside individual
nulls reflects that the Magyar confessional denominations (Reformed, Roman
Catholic, Unitarian) act collectively as a bloc predictor: when all three are
included alongside \texttt{pct\_orthodox}, the bloc's shared variance is
distributed across correlated predictors. The original M1 \texttt{pct\_maghiari}
performs the same labour more parsimoniously by treating the bloc as a unit.

**H2 (AUR and SOS ~ Pentecostal)** — both null ($p = 0.624$ and $p = 0.292$
respectively). The Pentecostal mobilisation thesis, influential in comparative
studies of Latin American and sub-Saharan African evangelical politics
[@Mudde2017], does not transfer to Romania. At 2.1\% of the national population,
the Romanian Pentecostal community does not constitute a distinct nationalist
electoral base at the county level, at least not at the spatial resolution
available here.

**H3 (USR ~ secular bloc)** — null ($\hat{\beta} = +0.12$, $p = 0.590$).
The sign is in the hypothesised direction but falls well short of significance.
Urban concentration (captured by the modernity index) already absorbs most of
the secular-reformist co-variation at the *județ* level.

**The single FDR-surviving finding** is a negative association between Greek
Catholic share and SOS vote ($\hat{\beta} = -0.173$, $q = 0.083$).
Greek Catholic counties — Bistrița-Năsăud, Cluj, Bihor, Satu Mare, Alba —
cluster in the historically Habsburg Transylvanian arc where the Greek Catholic
Church played a central role in Romanian national consciousness and literacy
[@Enyedi2005]. These counties are characterised by higher education, mixed
ethnicity, and historically more pluralist political culture. The negative
relationship indicates that where Greek Catholic identity remains electorally
salient, SOS's sovereignist nationalism finds less fertile ground —
a confessional-cultural brake on the far-right that does not appear in
deindustrialisation or grievance indices.

# The Georgescu–Simion Transfer {#sec:transfer}

## Motivation and method

The November 2024 first-round presidential result for Călin Georgescu (annulled)
and the May 2025 first-round result for George Simion provide a natural
test of vote-bloc persistence across institutional discontinuity.
A simple correlation would conflate genuine bloc cohesion with shared structural
confounders: both candidates drew disproportionately from peripheral,
deindustrialised counties.

We apply the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL) theorem [@Frisch1933; @Lovell1963]:
residualise both the Georgescu vote share and the Simion vote share on the same
set of structural controls, then compute the correlation of the two residual vectors.
This partial correlation equals the OLS coefficient from a full regression of
Simion on Georgescu conditional on all controls.

The control set comprises eight predictors with pairwise VIF $< 10$:
grievance index, modernity index, demographic pressure index,
agricultural employment share, Magyar share, Roma share,
deindustrialisation index, and long-term unemployment rate.
Composite indices (grievance, modernity, demographic pressure) absorb the
collinear raw features while reducing the effective parameter count.

Standard errors on the partial correlation are obtained via a
non-parametric bootstrap ($B = 10\,000$ draws with replacement).
Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding is assessed using the Robustness Value
framework of @Cinelli2020.

## Results

```{r fig-transfer-scatter, fig.cap="Partial correlation scatter plot: Simion 2025 R1 residuals vs Georgescu 2024 R1 residuals, after removing shared structural variance (8 controls). Points coloured by voter-profile cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "07a_georgescu_simion_scatter.png"))
```

The raw county-level correlation between the two vote shares is $r = 0.884$
($p < 0.001$). After removing shared structural variance, the partial correlation
is $r_\text{partial} = 0.770$ (95\% bootstrap CI: $[0.649, 0.863]$, $p < 0.0001$).
The reduction from $r = 0.884$ to $r_\text{partial} = 0.770$ confirms that
structural confounders explain part of the co-movement, but a substantial
residual association remains.

```{r transfer-sensitivity-table}
sens_tab <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Statistic,                            ~Value,
  "Raw correlation $r$",                "0.884",
  "Partial correlation $r_\\text{p}$",  "0.770",
  "Bootstrap 95\\% CI",                 "[0.649, 0.863]",
  "$p$-value",                          "<0.0001",
  "Robustness Value (RV)",              "0.547"
)

knitr::kable(
  sens_tab,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Georgescu–Simion transfer: summary statistics.",
  escape   = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Statistic", "Value")
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

The Robustness Value $\text{RV} = 0.547$ indicates that an unmeasured confounder
would need to explain at least 54.7\% of the residual variance in *both*
the Georgescu vote *and* the Simion vote (conditional on all eight included controls)
to fully account for the partial correlation. This is a demanding threshold:
for comparison, the strongest included control (deindustrialisation index) accounts
for approximately 30\% of the residual variance in each outcome. The finding is
therefore robust to moderate omitted variable bias.

```{r fig-transfer-clusters, fig.cap="Cluster-stratified partial correlations and 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The transfer signal is consistent across all clusters, though attenuated in Insula Capitalei ($n=2$, treat with caution)."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "07a_partial_corr_clusters.png"))
```

## Interpretation

The persistent partial correlation confirms the existence of a spatially
stable nationalist-populist electoral bloc at the county level, whose cohesion
is not reducible to the structural predictors included in the model.
This is consistent with network-mobilisation theories of populist vote
transfer [@Mudde2017; @Norris2019], in which social and online networks
sustain bloc identity across candidate discontinuities.

The ecological nature of the data precludes individual-level inference
(ecological fallacy caveat applies). The finding is best interpreted as evidence
that *counties* that mobilised strongly for Georgescu subsequently mobilised
strongly for Simion, net of structural conditions, rather than as evidence
that individual Georgescu voters switched to Simion.

# Electoral Dynamics 2020–2025 {#sec:temporal}

## Parliamentary swing: 2020 vs 2024

We construct vote-share swing vectors $\Delta Y_{i,p} = s_{i,p,2024} - s_{i,p,2020}$
for each party $p$ in county $i$, using Senate (Chamber of Senators) results for
comparability. Vâlcea county is excluded from swing regressions due to missing
2020 data ($n = 40$ for OLS models). Each party-specific swing is regressed on the
eight standardised structural controls used throughout this paper, with HC3-robust
standard errors.

```{r fig-swing-heatmap, fig.cap="Mean party-specific vote share swing (2020--2024 Senate) by voter-profile cluster. Positive values indicate a cluster-level gain between elections."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "09a_swing_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r fig-aur-swing, fig.cap="AUR 2020--2024 Senate swing vs deindustrialisation index, coloured by cluster. OLS fit shown."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "09a_aur_swing_scatter.png"))
```

```{r swing-ols-table}
swing_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "09a_swing_2020_2024.csv"),
                             show_col_types = FALSE)

swing_tab <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Party, ~`$R^2$`, ~`adj-$R^2$`, ~`Key predictor ($p<0.10$)`,
  "AUR",   "0.585", "0.477", "Dem. pressure (β=+0.016, p=0.039); −Magyar share (p=0.001)",
  "PSD",   "0.315", "0.138", "None (p<0.10)",
  "PNL",   "0.409", "0.257", "−Modernity (β=−0.048, p=0.037); +Magyar share (p<0.001)",
  "USR",   "0.533", "0.413", "+Agri. employment (β=+0.017, p=0.007)",
  "Other", "0.251", "0.058", "+Long-term unemployment (p=0.081)"
)

knitr::kable(
  swing_tab,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "OLS swing models: structural predictors of 2020--2024 Senate vote share change. $n = 40$ (Vâlcea excluded). HC3 standard errors.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

AUR's geographic swing is the most structurally explicable ($R^2 = 0.585$):
gains are concentrated in counties with high demographic pressure and low Magyar
share, consistent with AUR's ethnically homogeneous rural mobilisation strategy.
USR losses correlate with agricultural employment — the party haemorrhaged most
in rural peripheries it never fully consolidated — while PNL's moderate $R^2 = 0.409$
reflects loss of ground in more modern counties, possibly to USR absorption of
the urban reformist vote.

**Compositional robustness check.** Standard OLS on party-specific swing vectors
violates the zero-sum constraint ($\sum_p \Delta Y_{i,p} = 0$). We verify
robustness using a centred log-ratio (CLR) transformation [@Aitchison1986]:
$\text{clr}(\mathbf{y}) = \log(\mathbf{y}) - \bar{\log(\mathbf{y})}$, computing
CLR differences between 2024 and 2020 shares as compositionally valid swing vectors.
CLR swing $R^2$ values for AUR (0.486), USR (0.547), PSD (0.249), and PNL (0.245)
are directionally consistent with OLS, and the key predictors (demographic pressure
for AUR; agricultural employment for USR) retain significance under the compositional
specification. The PNL CLR $R^2$ diverges modestly (0.245 vs OLS 0.409), likely
reflecting greater sensitivity to the zero-replacement correction applied to AUR's
near-zero 2020 share. We note this as a limitation and report OLS estimates as
primary with CLR as a sensitivity check.

**Spatial heterogeneity of the deindustrialisation effect.** To test whether the
deindustrialisation–AUR relationship is concentrated in the *Moldova Profundă*
cluster — the region with the deepest industrial legacy loss — we add an
interaction term ($z_{\text{deindustrial}} \times \mathbb{1}_{\text{Moldova}}$)
to the AUR swing OLS. The interaction coefficient is $\hat{\beta} = -0.044$
($p = 0.573$), providing no evidence that the deindustrialisation effect is
amplified or attenuated within Moldova Profundă relative to other clusters.
The structural relationship is spatially uniform across cluster types.

## The 2024–2025 presidential arc

The three-election presidential sequence — Georgescu R1 (November 2024, annulled),
Simion R1 (May 2025), Simion/Dan R2 (June 2025) — provides a rare natural
experiment in populist electoral geography. Georgescu received 21.0\% nationally
in R1; Simion received 38.7\% in R1 and 44.8\% in R2; Dan received 55.2\% in R2.

```{r fig-presidential-arc, fig.cap="Presidential vote share trajectories at county level: Georgescu R1 2024 $\\to$ Simion R1 2025 $\\to$ Simion R2 2025. Each line is one county; colour indicates cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "09b_presidential_arc.png"))
```

```{r fig-runoff-consolidation, fig.cap="Dan consolidation ratio (Dan R2 / (1 $-$ Simion R1)) by county, with Simion R1 share on the x-axis. Dashed line at ratio = 1.0."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "09b_runoff_consolidation.png"))
```

The raw county-level correlation $r = 0.884$ between Georgescu R1 and Simion R1 confirms geographic continuity of the nationalist-populist bloc, as documented in Section \@ref(sec:transfer).
The Simion R1-to-R2 correlation is even tighter ($r = 0.970$), indicating near-perfect spatial consistency in the nationalist constituency during the runoff.

Table \@ref(tab:runoff-cluster-table) decomposes the R2 consolidation by cluster.
The Dan consolidation ratio $\rho_i = \text{Dan R2}_i / (1 - \text{Simion R1}_i)$
measures what share of the non-Simion R1 pool ultimately supported Dan.

```{r runoff-cluster-table}
arc_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "09b_presidential_arc.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

cluster_arc <- arc_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(cluster_short) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `Simion R1 (\\%)` = sprintf("%.1f", mean(simion_r1, na.rm=TRUE)*100),
    `Simion R2 (\\%)` = sprintf("%.1f", mean(simion_r2, na.rm=TRUE)*100),
    `R2 gain (pp)`    = sprintf("+%.1f", mean(simion_r2_gain, na.rm=TRUE)*100),
    `Dan consol. ratio` = sprintf("%.3f", mean(dan_of_anti, na.rm=TRUE))
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(Cluster = cluster_short)

knitr::kable(
  cluster_arc,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "R2 consolidation by voter-profile cluster. Dan consolidation ratio = Dan R2 / (1 $-$ Simion R1). Values above 1.0 imply Dan received more than the full non-Simion pool.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

Dan's consolidation was most efficient in *Arcul Identitar* (ratio = 0.953),
where the high Magyar and minority share produced a near-complete anti-Simion
mobilisation. The weakest consolidation is in *Câmpia Uitată* (0.823),
the cluster characterised by the deepest economic deprivation and lowest
engagement with the reformist political offer. The cluster mean differences
are consistent with the view that Dan's R2 performance represented a
*defensive* coalition — unified against Simion rather than by a positive programme —
that found its geographic floor precisely where structural grievance was highest.

## Annulment effect on Simion R1 turnout

The Constitutional Court's annulment of the November 2024 election was widely
debated as a potential mobilisation trigger: counties with high Georgescu support
might have either *mobilised in indignation* (higher Simion R1 turnout than
structural predictors would suggest) or been *demobilised by disillusionment*
(lower turnout). We test this by regressing Simion R1 turnout on the eight
structural controls (Model A) to obtain structural residuals, then assessing
whether Georgescu R1 share predicts those residuals (FWL partial correlation
and direct Model B coefficient).

The partial correlation is $r_{\text{partial}} = -0.123$ ($p = 0.437$), and
Model B's direct Georgescu coefficient is $\hat{\beta} = -0.011$ ($p = 0.543$),
with 95\% CI $[-0.045,\; 0.023]$ — the interval spans both the indignation and
abstention hypotheses without excluding zero. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-annulment-scatter)
visualises the scatter.

We extend the test to the *compositional* dimension: does the Georgescu fraction
of the 2024 nationalist-populist bloc ($\text{georgescu\_r1} / \text{bloc}_{2024}$)
predict anomalous nationalist *uplift* ($\Delta = \text{Simion R1}_{2025} -
[\text{Georgescu R1} + \text{Simion R1}_{2024}]$) beyond structural predictors?
The FWL partial correlation is $r_{\text{partial}} = -0.259$ ($p = 0.098$) and the
direct coefficient is $\hat{\beta} = -0.0049$ ($p = 0.165$) — both null at conventional
thresholds. The negative direction is consistent with the turnout test and argues
against a systematic indignation effect in counties that were most exposed to the
annulment controversy.

These two null results together constitute a *positive* finding: the 2025 first-round
outcome was structurally continuous with prior elections. The Constitutional Court
annulment did not produce a detectable county-level deviation — in either aggregate
turnout or bloc composition — from what the structural geography would have predicted
in its absence.

```{r fig-annulment-scatter, fig.cap="(Left) Simion R1 2025 turnout residual (actual $-$ structural prediction) vs Georgescu R1 2024 share, coloured by cluster. Dashed OLS trend; $r_{\\text{partial}} = -0.123$, $p = 0.437$. (Right) Model B coefficient plot."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "09c_annulment_scatter.png"))
```

# The Ghost Electorate {#sec:ghost}

## Definition and data

Romania's permanent electoral rolls systematically over-count the adult resident
population, primarily because the Central Electoral Registry retains records of
deceased persons and long-term emigrants until administratively deregistered.
We define the *Ghost Electorate Ratio* (GER) for county $i$ as:

$$\text{GER}_i = \frac{E_i - P^{18+}_i}{E_i}$$

where $E_i$ is the number of enrolled voters (AEP, 2024 parliamentary Senate rolls)
and $P^{18+}_i$ is the estimated resident population aged 18 and over.

$P^{18+}_i$ is derived from Eurostat dataset \texttt{demo\_r\_pjanaggr3} (NUTS-3,
reference year 2021):

$$P^{18+}_i \approx Y^{15\text{–}64}_i \times (1 - \hat{\alpha}) + Y^{65+}_i$$

where $\hat{\alpha} = (Y^{15} + Y^{16} + Y^{17})_{\text{RO}} / Y^{15\text{–}64}_{\text{RO}} = 0.0501$
is the national-level share of 15–17-year-olds within the 15–64 age group
(Eurostat \texttt{demo\_r\_d2jan}, 2021). This approximation introduces a bounded
imprecision of $< 1$ percentage point and is flagged as a limitation of the approach.

## Results

```{r fig-ghost-cluster, fig.cap="Left: Ghost Electorate Ratio (2024 Senate) by voter-profile cluster. Right: GER trajectories across four elections by cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "10a_ghost_electorate_cluster.png"))
```

```{r fig-ghost-correlates, fig.cap="GER vs permanent emigration rate (left) and GDP per capita (right), coloured by cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "10b_ger_correlates.png"))
```

```{r fig-ghost-ranked, fig.cap="Ghost Electorate Ratio by county, ranked ascending. Dashed line: national mean."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "10c_ger_ranked.png"))
```

```{r ghost-summary-table}
ger_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "10a_ghost_electorate.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

ghost_tab <- ger_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(cluster_short) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `Mean GER 2020` = sprintf("%.3f", mean(`ger_2020 parl`, na.rm=TRUE)),
    `Mean GER 2024` = sprintf("%.3f", mean(`ger_2024 parl`, na.rm=TRUE)),
    `Mean emigration rate` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(emigrants_permanent_rate, na.rm=TRUE))
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(Cluster = cluster_short)

knitr::kable(
  ghost_tab,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Ghost Electorate Ratio by cluster (parliamentary elections) and mean permanent emigration rate (per 1000 residents).",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

The national mean GER for the 2024 parliamentary rolls is 0.164 (SD = 0.058),
implying that approximately one in six registered voters in Romania is a ghost.
The ratio has remained stable between 2020 (mean = 0.165) and 2024, confirming
chronic administrative under-purging. Presidential rolls show systematically lower
GER (mean ≈ 0.127), consistent with BEC applying supplementary deregistration
procedures before presidential elections.

An OLS regression of GER on the full structural control set achieves $R^2 = 0.680$
(adjusted $R^2 = 0.590$), with permanent emigration rate as the sole predictor
significant at $p < 0.001$ ($\hat{\beta} = 0.033$, HC3 SE). This confirms
that the ghost electorate is primarily a *migration artefact*: counties that
disproportionately export population retain the highest roll inflation.

*Moldova Profundă* exhibits the highest GER (Vaslui: 0.348, Iași: 0.260, Bacău: 0.245),
all among Romania's leading emigration sources. At the other extreme, Ilfov
(0.084) and Giurgiu (0.047) reflect the Bucharest metropolitan periphery,
where in-migration has brought resident population close to or above roll size,
generating near-zero or negative ghost ratios.

The electoral implication is that turnout percentages in high-GER counties are
systematically deflated relative to actual participation. A county reporting
40\% turnout on inflated rolls may represent substantially higher actual
participation among the resident voting-age population — a measurement artefact
that should be corrected in any cross-county turnout analysis.

## Turnout deflation: formal test

We formalise this implication with an OLS model regressing reported turnout on
GER and the eight structural controls:

$$\text{turnout}_i = \alpha + \beta_{\text{GER}} \cdot \text{GER}_i + \boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{z}_i + \varepsilon_i$$

```{r turnout-deflation-table}
td_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "10b_turnout_deflation.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)

td_summary <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Statistic,                                    ~Value,
  "OLS $R^2$",                                   "0.746",
  "Adjusted $R^2$",                              "0.664",
  "$n$",                                         "42",
  "GER $\\hat{\\beta}$ (std.)",                  "$-0.008$",
  "GER SE",                                      "0.007",
  "GER $p$-value",                               "0.262",
  "Mean roll-based turnout",                     "46.4\\%",
  "Mean effective turnout (voted/pop$_{18+}$)",  "55.5\\%",
  "Mean deflation (effective $-$ roll-based)",   "$+9.1$ pp"
)

knitr::kable(
  td_summary,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Turnout deflation test. OLS of reported 2024 parliamentary turnout on GER and eight structural controls (HC3 SE). Effective turnout uses estimated 18+ population as denominator.",
  escape   = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Statistic", "Value")
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position"), font_size = 10)
```

Two results stand out. First, *reported* turnout is on average 9.1 percentage points
lower than *effective* turnout (votes cast relative to resident adult population),
purely because of GER inflation in the denominator. Second — and more surprising —
GER is not a significant predictor of *cross-county variation* in reported turnout
once structural controls are included ($\hat{\beta} = -0.008$, $p = 0.262$).
This indicates that the ghost electorate is approximately uniformly distributed
across the participation gradient: high-GER counties are not differentially more
or less likely to turn out than low-GER counties once economic and demographic
structure is controlled. The measurement artefact is a *level shift* (inflating
the denominator everywhere), not a *structural confounder* of the turnout pattern.

# Spatial Robustness {#sec:spatial}

## Motivation

All models reported so far use OLS or its derivatives under the assumption of
spatially independent errors. Romanian counties are geographically contiguous;
structural spillovers (labour mobility, media markets, political networks) and
electoral diffusion effects (social contagion in bloc mobilisation) may induce
positive spatial autocorrelation in model residuals. Ignoring this would understate
standard errors and inflate effective degrees of freedom.

We use Moran's $I$ statistic [@Anselin1988] to test for spatial autocorrelation
in OLS residuals from the three main models, and fit a generalised method of
moments spatial lag model [@Kelejian1999] for the AUR swing equation where the
Lagrange multiplier test indicates spatial lag dependence.

Spatial weights are queen contiguity (second-order adjacency is considered but
queen first-order provides better theoretical grounding for electoral diffusion),
row-standardised, derived from Eurostat GISCO NUTS-3 boundaries (2021, 1:10M).

## Results

```{r fig-romania-map, fig.cap="Three-panel choropleth of Romanian NUTS-3 units: (left) voter-profile cluster assignment; (centre) Ghost Electorate Ratio 2024; (right) AUR 2020--2024 Senate swing. Computed from GISCO NUTS-3 boundaries (Eurostat 2021)."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "11a_romania_map.png"))
```

```{r fig-moran-scatter, fig.cap="Moran scatter plots (standardised OLS residuals vs spatial lag) for three models. Positive quadrants (HH, LL) indicate clustering; negative quadrants indicate spatial outliers. Points coloured by voter-profile cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "11b_moran_scatter.png"))
```

```{r spatial-robustness-table}
spat_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "11a_spatial_robustness.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)

spat_tab <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Model,                       ~`Moran $I$`, ~`$p_{\\text{sim}}$`, ~`$z$`,     ~`LM-lag $p$`, ~`$\\hat{\\rho}$ (SLM)`, ~`SLM pseudo-$R^2$`,
  "AUR swing",                  "0.119",        "0.087",              "1.400",    "0.002",         "0.640",                  "0.707",
  "GER",                        "0.137",        "0.060",              "1.664",    "—",             "—",                      "—",
  "Georgescu transfer ($e_G$)", "0.071",        "0.150",              "0.987",    "—",             "—",                      "—",
  "Simion transfer ($e_S$)",    "$-0.068$",     "0.349",              "$-0.458$", "—",             "—",                      "—"
)

knitr::kable(
  spat_tab,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Spatial robustness diagnostics. Moran's $I$ computed on OLS residuals under queen contiguity weights (row-standardised). $p_{\\text{sim}}$: randomisation inference (999 permutations). Spatial lag model fitted only for AUR swing where LM-lag indicates lag dependence ($p = 0.002$) and LM-error does not ($p = 0.278$).",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```

Three conclusions follow from Table \@ref(tab:spatial-robustness-table) and
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-moran-scatter).

*The AUR swing and GER equations show marginal positive spatial autocorrelation.*
Moran's $I$ is 0.119 ($p = 0.087$) and 0.137 ($p = 0.060$) respectively,
indicating that OLS standard errors are moderately understated. The spatial lag
model for AUR swing confirms lag dependence: $\hat{\rho} = 0.640$ ($p < 0.01$),
and pseudo-$R^2$ rises from 0.585 to 0.707. This spatial lag coefficient implies
that counties whose neighbours experienced large AUR gains also gained — consistent
with an electoral diffusion or social-contagion mechanism operating at the
sub-regional scale beyond what structural predictors capture.

*The substantive findings on structural predictors are robust to spatial
correction.* The OLS and SLM coefficients for demographic pressure and Magyar
share maintain their signs and relative magnitudes, though absolute values halve
when spatial dependence is absorbed by the lag term. The structural story
(demographic pressure drives AUR gains; Magyar share suppresses them) is not
an artefact of spatial autocorrelation.

*The Georgescu–Simion transfer signal is spatially random* ($I = 0.071$,
$p = 0.150$ for $e_G$; $I = -0.068$, $p = 0.349$ for $e_S$). This is the
most important spatial finding: the bloc persistence documented in
Section \@ref(sec:transfer) is geographically diffuse and not driven by spatial
clustering in the residuals. The nationalist-populist bloc is a nationwide
phenomenon that does not operate through local spatial contagion alone.

# Robustness of the Cluster Solution {#sec:robustness}

A concern with hierarchical clustering is sensitivity to the choice of $k$.
We assess this by refitting Ward clustering on the PCA scores for $k \in \{4, 5, 6\}$
and recording: (i) the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between the alternative and the
primary $k = 5$ solution; (ii) the AUR swing OLS $R^2$ under each $k$; and
(iii) the Georgescu–Simion transfer partial correlation.

```{r cluster-k-robustness-table}
kdf <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "12a_cluster_k_robustness.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE)

kdf_display <- kdf |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `ARI vs $k=5$`         = dplyr::if_else(k == 5, "—", sprintf("%.3f", ARI_vs_k5)),
    `AUR swing $R^2$`      = sprintf("%.3f", AUR_swing_R2),
    `Transfer $r_{\\text{partial}}$` = sprintf("%.3f", transfer_r_partial)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(k, `ARI vs $k=5$`, `AUR swing $R^2$`,
                `Transfer $r_{\\text{partial}}$`)

knitr::kable(
  kdf_display,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Cluster solution robustness: ARI vs primary $k=5$, AUR swing OLS $R^2$, and Georgescu--Simion transfer partial correlation, for $k \\in \\{4, 5, 6\\}$. ARI computed via adjusted Rand index between refitted Ward solution and primary $k=5$ labels.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 10)
```

Table \@ref(tab:cluster-k-robustness-table) shows that the ARI between $k = 4$ and
$k = 5$ is 0.721, and between $k = 6$ and $k = 5$ is 0.762, indicating that
approximately three-quarters of county assignments are preserved under alternative
partitions. The AUR swing $R^2$ (0.585) and transfer partial correlation (0.783)
are *identical* across all three $k$ values — because both regressions use only
structural controls and contain no cluster fixed effects, meaning the structural
variance decomposition is by construction independent of how counties are partitioned.
The table therefore confirms that the main findings do not depend on the particular
cluster solution used to label the data.

# Conditional Projections {#sec:projections}

The analyses above are retrospective: they describe what happened in 2020–2025 and
why. This section extends them forward under explicitly stated structural assumptions,
producing conditional projections rather than forecasts. Three conditions frame every
result in this section:

- **C1** — George Simion is the nationalist candidate in any future presidential election.
- **C2** — A single reformist candidate consolidates the anti-Simion pool at the efficiency
  observed in 2025.
- **C3** — Structural conditions (deindustrialisation, demographic pressure, ethnic composition)
  remain at their 2025 values.

Violations of any of these conditions — a Simion–AUR split, a fragmented reformist field,
or accelerated deindustrialisation in eastern counties — are the primary sources of
projection error and are not modelled here.

## Bayesian hierarchical model of AUR swing

The OLS swing model ($R^2 = 0.585$, Section \@ref(sec:temporal)) treats the 40
counties as exchangeable observations. This ignores the cluster structure: county
predictions from *Moldova Profundă* should be shrunk toward the Moldova Profundă
cluster mean, not toward the global mean. We reformulate the model as a Bayesian
hierarchical regression with cluster-level random intercepts:

$$\text{sw\_AUR}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$$
$$\mu_i = \alpha_{j[i]} + \sum_{k} \beta_k \cdot z_{x_{ik}}$$
$$\alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(\bar{\alpha},\, \sigma_\alpha), \quad
  \beta_k \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.02), \quad
  \sigma, \sigma_\alpha \sim \text{HalfNormal}(0.02)$$

Priors are weakly informative: $\sigma = 0.02$ on a standardised predictor
corresponds to a prior belief that a one-SD shift in any structural predictor
is unlikely to produce more than a 4 pp swing (two prior SDs), which is
deliberately conservative relative to the observed range.

Estimation uses NUTS via PyMC [@Salvatier2016], 4 chains $\times$ 2{,}000
post-warmup draws. Convergence is assessed by $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and
$\text{ESS}_\text{bulk} > 400$ on all $\beta$ parameters.

```{r bayes-convergence}
bsum <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "14a_bayes_summary.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)

beta_rows <- bsum |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^beta_", parameter)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(parameter,
      beta_idx_grievance              = "Grievance index",
      beta_idx_modernity              = "Modernity index",
      beta_idx_demographic_pressure   = "Demographic pressure",
      beta_pct_employment_agriculture = "Agri. employment",
      beta_pct_maghiari               = "Magyar \\%",
      beta_pct_romi                   = "Roma \\%",
      beta_gva_deindustrial_index     = "Deindustrialisation",
      beta_long_term_unemployment_rate= "LT unemployment"
    ),
    `$\\hat{\\beta}$ (\\texttimes 100)` = sprintf("%+.3f", mean * 100),
    `90\\% CI`   = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q05 * 100, q95 * 100),
    `$\\hat{R}$` = sprintf("%.4f", rhat),
    ESS          = as.integer(ess)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(Predictor,
                `$\\hat{\\beta}$ (\\texttimes 100)`,
                `90\\% CI`, `$\\hat{R}$`, ESS)

knitr::kable(
  beta_rows,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Bayesian hierarchical AUR swing model: fixed-effect posteriors.
              $\\hat{\\beta}$ scaled $\\times 100$ (pp per $+1$ SD predictor).
              90\\% credible intervals. $\\hat{R} < 1.01$ and ESS $> 400$
              indicate chain convergence.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```

```{r fig-bayes-coefs, fig.cap="Posterior fixed-effect estimates for the Bayesian hierarchical AUR swing model. Bars = posterior mean; whiskers = 90\\% credible interval. Red = CI excludes zero."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "14a_bayes_posterior_coefs.png"))
```

```{r fig-bayes-preds, fig.cap="County-level 90\\% posterior predictive intervals, sorted by posterior mean swing. Dots = observed swing, coloured by cluster. The hierarchical model shrinks extreme county predictions toward their cluster mean, widening intervals for counties that deviate from their cluster's structural pattern."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "14a_bayes_pred_intervals.png"))
```

The hierarchical model reproduces the OLS substantive findings: demographic
pressure and Magyar share are the dominant fixed-effect predictors, with
deindustrialisation marginally credible. The key added value is interval
calibration: OLS prediction intervals assume homoscedastic, exchangeable residuals,
whereas the hierarchical model accounts for residual clustering — counties in
*Moldova Profundă* have systematically higher swing than the structural prediction
alone implies, a pattern the random intercept absorbs rather than misattributing
to the fixed predictors.

## Swing county ranking

A *swing county* in a future Simion vs reformist runoff is one where the projected
Simion R2 share is close to 50\% and where that projection is uncertain. We
formalise both dimensions. Using the transfer model calibrated on 2025 R2 actuals
($R^2 = 0.970$), we obtain bootstrap-projected R2 shares for each county ($B = 5{,}000$
pairs bootstrap). The composite swing score is:

$$\text{composite}_i = \frac{|\hat{y}_i - 0.50|}{\text{PI}_{80\%,i}}$$

where $\hat{y}_i$ is the bootstrap median projected share and $\text{PI}_{80\%}$ is the
80\% prediction interval width. A lower composite score indicates higher swing potential —
the county is close to the tipping point *and* that proximity is genuine rather than
spuriously precise.

```{r swing-county-table}
sc <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "14b_swing_counties.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

sc_display <- sc |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Pred R2`   = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", predicted_simion_r2 * 100),
    `Obs R2`    = sprintf("%.1f\\%%", simion_r2 * 100),
    `80\\% PI width` = sprintf("%.1f pp", bootstrap_width * 100),
    `Distance`  = sprintf("%.1f pp", swing_score * 100),
    Cluster     = cluster_short
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(County = judet, Cluster,
                `Pred R2`, `Obs R2`, `Distance`, `80\\% PI width`)

knitr::kable(
  sc_display,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Top 10 swing counties by composite score (competitive $\\times$ uncertain).
              Conditional on C1–C3. Distance = $|\\hat{y} - 0.50|$;
              80\\% PI width from $B = 5{,}000$ pairs bootstrap.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```

```{r fig-swing-counties, fig.cap="(Left) 80\\% bootstrap prediction intervals for the top 15 swing counties. Bars = PI; diamonds = observed 2025 R2; dashed line = 50\\% tipping point. (Right) Swing space: horizontal axis = prediction uncertainty, vertical axis = distance from 50\\%. Lower-left counties are highest swing potential."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "14b_swing_county_ranking.png"))
```

The top swing counties are concentrated in *Câmpia Uitată* (5 of the top 10) and
*Arcul Identitar* (2 of the top 10). The Câmpia Uitată counties are competitive
because they sit structurally between the nationalist core (high deindustrialisation,
high demographic pressure) and the reformist fringe (residual PNL organisation);
their 2025 R2 observed shares cluster close to 50\%. The Arcul Identitar entries
(Bistrița-Năsăud, Maramureș) are competitive because the Magyar minority share
locally depresses Simion's ceiling while deindustrialisation sustains his floor.

## Presidential bloc projection

The presidential bloc model estimates how the 2025 R1 → R2 transfer generalises
to a future election under conditions C1–C3. The transfer OLS fits cleanly
($R^2 = 0.970$): Simion's R2 share is almost entirely predictable from his R1
share and structural controls, with $\hat{\beta}_{\text{R1}} = 0.093$
($p < 0.001$). The Dan consolidation model reaches $R^2 = 0.699$; the only
significant structural predictor of the anti-Simion consolidation ratio is
Magyar share ($\hat{\beta} = +0.031$, $p = 0.025$) and demographic pressure
($\hat{\beta} = -0.033$, $p = 0.027$): the reformist candidate consolidates
better in ethnically mixed counties and worse where demographic stress is highest.

```{r presidential-bloc-table}
pb <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "14c_presidential_bloc.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

pb_cluster <- pb |>
  dplyr::group_by(cluster_short) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `Obs R2 (\\%)`       = sprintf("%.1f", mean(simion_r2) * 100),
    `Proj R2 (\\%)`      = sprintf("%.1f", mean(sim_proj_median) * 100),
    `90\\% PI`           = sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]",
                                   mean(sim_proj_q05) * 100,
                                   mean(sim_proj_q95) * 100),
    `Genuine uncert.`    = sprintf("%d/%d", sum(uncertain), dplyr::n())
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(Cluster = cluster_short)

knitr::kable(
  pb_cluster,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "Presidential bloc projection by cluster. Obs R2 = 2025 observed Simion R2 share (cluster mean). Proj R2 = bootstrap median projection. 90\\% PI = mean county-level interval. Genuine uncert.\\ = counties whose 90\\% PI straddles the 50\\% tipping point.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```

```{r fig-presidential-bloc, fig.cap="(Left) Transfer model: Simion R1 to R2, with 50\\%/90\\% bootstrap projection bands. (Right) County-level 90\\% projection intervals sorted by projected share; gold verticals mark counties with genuine 50\\% uncertainty."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG_DIR, "14c_presidential_bloc.png"))
```

The mean projected Simion R2 share is 47.1\% (90\% PI: 44.9\%–49.2\%), exactly
matching the 2025 observed mean — which is expected since the model is calibrated
on 2025 actuals. The projection's value is not in the national aggregate but in the
geographic distribution: *Moldova Profundă* and *Câmpia Uitată* are projected to
remain above 50\% for Simion, while *Arcul Identitar* and *Insula Capitalei*
remain well below it. Nine of 42 counties have 90\% projection intervals that
straddle the 50\% tipping point — these are the counties where a change in C2
(reformist consolidation efficiency) would be decisive.

**What would change the projection.** The model is most sensitive to the
consolidation assumption (C2). In 2025, Dan captured 95.3\% of the non-Simion
R1 pool in *Arcul Identitar* but only 82.3\% in *Câmpia Uitată*. A 5 pp
improvement in reformist consolidation in *Câmpia Uitată* alone — bringing
it from 0.823 to 0.873 — would flip an estimated 4–6 counties currently
projected as Simion-leaning into genuine toss-ups.

# Discussion {#sec:discussion}

## Structural geography and electoral fragmentation

The five-cluster typology reveals a Romanian electoral geography organised along
two intersecting axes: a *development gradient* (Insula Capitalei → Centrele
Dinamice → Câmpia Uitată → Moldova Profundă) and an *ethnic-confessional axis*
(Arcul Identitar). The development gradient maps closely onto the spatial
inequality literature on post-communist transition [@Holesch2021], while the
ethnic axis reflects the persistence of communal identity as an electoral organiser
[@Enyedi2005].

The deindustrialisation index emerges as the most consistent structural predictor
across multiple analyses: it is the variable most responsible for Moldova Profundă's
high AUR and POT shares (cluster-ANOVA), the dominant cross-party coefficient in
the Dirichlet regression, and a major control in the transfer analysis.
This converges with findings on deindustrialisation and radical-right voting
in Western Europe [@Oesch2008; @Rooduijn2018] but with the important caveat
that in Romania the effect is diffuse across parties rather than channelled
specifically into a single anti-establishment outlet.

The Bayesian hierarchical model introduces a finding that complicates the
grievance narrative. The posterior mean for the grievance index on AUR swing is
$-0.029$ (90\% CI $[-0.045, -0.013]$), meaning that counties with *higher*
composite grievance show *lower* AUR growth, conditional on the remaining
predictors. A collinearity explanation can be ruled out: the correlation between
grievance and deindustrialisation is $r = -0.178$ ($p = 0.260$) and all
pairwise VIFs are below 2.5 [@Cinelli2020], confirming that the negative
grievance coefficient is a genuine conditional effect rather than a suppression
artefact. The substantive interpretation hinges on what the two indices capture
at the county level: deindustrialisation measures the *scale of manufacturing
loss since 2010* — an aspirational disappointment concentrated in counties that
once had industrial bases — whereas the grievance composite captures chronic,
multi-decade deprivation. The worst-off counties, where poverty and long-term
unemployment are highest, may exhibit structural electoral fatalism or continued
clientelistic attachment to PSD, which suppresses nationalist mobilisation
independently of deindustrialisation dynamics. This distinction echoes
@Rodríguez-Pose2018's argument that it is not absolute deprivation but
*relative decline* that energises populist voting — a mechanism better proxied
by the deindustrialisation index than by the static grievance composite.

## The limits of structural determinism

The Georgescu–Simion transfer analysis complicates a purely structural account.
A partial correlation of 0.770 after controlling for eight structural predictors
— with Robustness Value 0.547 — suggests that county-level bloc cohesion is not
fully determined by observable socio-economic geography.
The residual association could reflect: (a) unmeasured structural features
(e.g., social capital deficits, media exposure); (b) network effects and social
contagion operating below the county level; or (c) genuine ideological consistency
among Georgescu/Simion voters that persists independent of material conditions.
Distinguishing these mechanisms requires individual-level data that are not
currently available.

# Conclusion {#sec:conclusion}

Using county-level data for all 42 Romanian *județe*, this paper has shown:

1. Romanian counties organise into five structurally coherent voter-profile
   clusters whose electoral differentiation is statistically significant on held-out
   party vote shares (ANOVA $p < 0.001$ for five of seven parties); the solution
   is stable under alternative $k \in \{4, 6\}$ specifications (ARI $\geq 0.72$)
   and the main analytical findings are unchanged across $k$.
2. In a Dirichlet regression framework, deindustrialisation is the dominant
   cross-party structural predictor of vote share composition, followed by
   ethnic composition (for UDMR) and modernity (for SOS and UDMR); five
   coefficients survive Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction ($q < 0.10$);
   LOO Aitchison skill score = 0.179.
3. The county-level nationalist-populist electoral bloc — defined by support for
   Călin Georgescu in November 2024 — persists robustly into the May 2025
   Simion vote after controlling for structural confounders
   (partial $r = 0.770$, RV = 0.547).
4. AUR's 2020–2024 Senate swing is structurally explained ($R^2 = 0.585$), driven
   by demographic pressure and ethnic homogeneity; a spatial lag model raises
   pseudo-$R^2$ to 0.707 ($\hat{\rho} = 0.640$), confirming a neighbourhood
   contagion mechanism while leaving the structural story intact.
   Dan's 2025 runoff consolidation was most efficient in ethnically mixed
   Transylvania (ratio = 0.953) and weakest in the most deprived flatland cluster
   (*Câmpia Uitată*, ratio = 0.823).
5. The ghost electorate ratio averages 16.4\% nationally (2024 parliamentary
   rolls), almost entirely predicted by emigration rates ($R^2 = 0.680$), and
   inflates the turnout denominator by 9.1 pp on average — but does not
   independently predict cross-county turnout variation once structural controls
   are included ($p = 0.262$), implying the artefact is a level shift rather than
   a structural confounder.
6. Moran's $I$ on transfer residuals is indistinguishable from zero ($p > 0.14$),
   establishing that the nationalist-populist bloc cohesion is geographically
   diffuse and not a local spatial contagion effect.
7. The Constitutional Court annulment of Georgescu's 2024 result left no
   statistically detectable county-level mobilisation imprint on either
   Simion R1 turnout ($\hat{\beta} = -0.011$, $p = 0.543$) or the composition
   of nationalist uplift ($r_{\text{partial}} = -0.259$, $p = 0.098$).
   Both tests are null at conventional thresholds; taken together they establish
   that the 2025 first-round was structurally continuous with prior elections —
   the annulment did not produce detectable county-level deviation from what
   the structural geography would have predicted in its absence.
8. A Bayesian hierarchical reformulation (4 chains $\times$ 4000 draws,
   max R-hat $= 1.001$) identifies long-term unemployment as the sole positive
   structural predictor of AUR growth and reveals a negative grievance coefficient
   (posterior mean $= -0.029$, 90\% CI $[-0.045, -0.013]$), consistent with
   @Rodríguez-Pose2018's relative-decline thesis: it is aspirationally disappointed
   deindustrialised counties, not the chronically deprived ones, that drive
   nationalist mobilisation. Under the 2025 calibrated bloc transfer rates,
   a conditional projection places mean Simion R2 at 47.1\% (90\% PI: 44.9\%–49.2\%),
   with 9 of 42 counties in genuine uncertainty; a 5 pp improvement in reformist
   consolidation in *Câmpia Uitată* would flip 4–6 of these counties.

These findings contribute to the growing literature on structural drivers of
populist voting in post-communist democracies and underscore that Romania's
2024–2025 electoral fragmentation is not a temporary shock but the expression
of durable spatial inequalities.

**Limitations.** All analyses are ecological: inferences about individual voters
require survey data with spatial identifiers. The sample of 42 counties limits
the power of Dirichlet regression and prevents the inclusion of rich cluster-fixed
effects. The 18+ population estimates introduce a bounded approximation error
($< 1$ pp) from the 15–17 age-group correction; individual-year NUTS-3 age
data are not publicly available from Eurostat for Romanian counties.
PNL local organisational network analysis remains pending conditional
on local election data.

# Appendix C — Dirichlet Regression Full Coefficient Table (M1) {-}

```{r appendix-dirichlet-full}
coef_df <- readr::read_csv(file.path(REP_DIR, "08a_dirichlet_coefs.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)

full_m1 <- coef_df |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "M1", term != "(Intercept)") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Party     = sub("t_", "", category),
    Predictor = dplyr::recode(term,
      z_grievance    = "Grievance",
      z_modernity    = "Modernity",
      z_magyari      = "\\% Magyar",
      z_deindustrial = "Deindustrial."
    ),
    `$\\hat{\\beta}$` = sprintf("%.3f",  estimate),
    SE                 = sprintf("%.3f",  se),
    `$z$`             = sprintf("%.2f",  z),
    `$p$`             = dplyr::case_when(
      is.na(p)  ~ "—",
      p < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE      ~ sprintf("%.3f", p)
    ),
    Sig = ifelse(is.na(sig), "—", as.character(sig))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(Party, Predictor, `$\\hat{\\beta}$`, SE, `$z$`, `$p$`, Sig)

knitr::kable(
  full_m1,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption  = "M1 Dirichlet regression: all non-intercept coefficients. ALR scale, reference = Other.",
  escape   = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "striped"),
                            font_size = 9)
```
